D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b000_.text: Last time, I left you at the door of the finance office, the box, and I promised I'd tell you what happens inside. So come in, sit down. Here's the first thing that happens in there. You're sitting across a little desk from a man in a nice tie. You agreed on the price of the car outside. You're tired, it's been three hours, and you reach in your purse or your jacket, and you say the words you've been proud of all week, I'm paying cash. And you think that's the end of the game. It's not. For the man in the nice tie, it's the beginning. I know, because for 26 years, I was the man in the nice tie. My name is Hector, I sold cars in Miami for 40 years, and from 1989 to 2015, I was the finance manager at Bird Road Auto Plaza. Today I'm going to tell you, from the other side of that desk, why a retiree should almost never walk in and just pay cash for a car.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b001_.text: It sounds backwards, I know. You were raised like me. If you can't pay cash, you can't afford it. And that's a good rule for a lot of things. For a car dealership, it's a gift to the dealer. I'm going to give you nine reasons with real numbers. And then the last one, the one nobody does. The one I used against Mrs. Shapiro. And the one you're going to use against them. Okay. Let me tell you about Coach Willis. June 2006, Coach Earl Willis had just retired after 34 years teaching PE and coaching baseball at a high school in Westchester. Big man, whistle-tan line on his neck, still wore the windbreaker with the school name on it. Everybody in Westchester knew Coach. Half the salesmen on our lot had played for him. And Coach walked into Bird Road Auto Plaza on a Saturday morning with a cashier's check folded in his shirt pocket. $26,000.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b002_.text: He'd been saving to buy his wife a new car the day he retired. And the first thing he said to the salesman before hello was, Son, I'm a cash buyer. I don't want any of your financing games. Let's make this quick. Coach thought he was being smart. Coach thought cash was power. And by the time he left our dealership that afternoon, Coach Willis had lost, I'm not exaggerating, a little over $6,000. And he shook my hand at the end. He said, Hector, you're a good man. I'll tell you exactly how he lost it, piece by piece, because every piece is one of the reasons. Reason number one. The moment you say cash, the dealer stops discounting. Remember Abe Feldman's four square from the last video? Price, trade, down payment, monthly payment, four boxes. When you finance at the dealership, there's a fifth box nobody draws, the finance office.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b003_.text: Because when you finance with us, the bank pays the dealership. It's called the reserve. I told you about it. The extra points on your rate. And the finance office also sells you products. Service contracts, gap, the protection packages. And a lot of that goes inside your payment where you can't see it. So when a salesman has a customer who's going to finance, he can give a little more on the price. $1,000 off, $1,500 off. Because he knows the box will make it back. But when you say cash, the fifth box closes. There's no reserve. There's no payment to hide things in. So the salesman's manager up in the tower says cash deal, hold the price. Don't give him anything. That's what happened to coach. The car was listed at $24,900. The salesman had permission to go down about $1,200 for a finance deal.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b004_.text: for coach because coach said cash in the first 10 seconds he went down 200 two hundred dollars and coach was happy because the kid who played second base for him in 1988 gave him 200 offers a favor 1200 minus 200 coach just lost his first thousand dollars and he didn't even sit down yet so what do you do you don't lie you just don't say how you're paying until the price is signed When they ask, are you paying cash or financing? You say, I haven't decided yet. Let's agree on the price first. That's the truth. You haven't decided. And after today, you really won't have. Reason number two, the rebates that only exist if you finance. This one makes people angry and they should be angry. A lot of times the factory, the car company itself puts money on the hood of a car, a rebate.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b005_.text: 2,000, 2,500, sometimes more. But read the small letters on the sign. Sometimes that money is only for customers who finance through the car company's own bank. The captive lender, we called it. Every big car company has its own bank. And they want the loans. So they pay you to take one. Coach Willis' car had a $2,500 bonus that month. Financing through the manufacturer's bank required. Coach paid cash. So Coach didn't get it, and nobody told him. Why would we? He said, I don't want any of your financing games. We respected his wishes. That's what I told myself anyway. My nephew Danny, he sells today in Douro, tells me it's even trickier now. Some dealers advertise a price online, a beautiful price, and in the fine print at the bottom, it says the price includes a dealer finance discount. $1,500, $2,000.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b006_.text: Which means, if you pay cash, the price goes up. The cash buyer pays more than the finance buyer for the same car on the same day. So before you go, you look at the manufacturer's website for the special offers on that exact car in your zip code. And you ask the salesman one simple thing. Is there any rebate or discount that requires financing? Write down what he says. If there is, we're going to use it. I'll show you how at the end. And while we're on what you say and when you say it, people ask me about the down payment. Hector, what if I'm not paying all cash, but I'm putting down half? 10,000 down? Same rule, different box. The down payment is one of Abe's four squares. And if the salesman knows you're putting 10,000 down, he knows the payment will be small. So he knows he has room and that room gets filled. Not with your benefit, with his.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b007_.text: So the down payment is the last thing you tell. Price first, in writing. Then trade, separately. Then at the very end you say, and I'll put this much down. And if you're not sure how much to put down, put down less. You can always pay more on the loan next month. You can't take back a down payment once it's in the dealer's bank. And one more from Danny from just last month. He says, now a lot of dealers ask for a deposit to hold the car. $500, $1,000 on your card. We'll hold it for you until tomorrow. There's another couple looking at it. And that deposit is a little hook in your lip because now you've paid something and people hate to lose what they already paid. If you ever give a deposit, and I'd rather you didn't, you get it in writing on the receipt, the word refundable, fully refundable, if I don't buy. And the date, and you ask them to sign it,

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b008_.text: Because I've seen deposits become very hard to get back. Very hard. It's always somebody's day off. Reason number three, where the cash came from. Now this is the part of Coach's story that still makes me sick, honestly. And it's the one that matters most for people our age. Coach didn't have $26,000 sitting in a savings account. Teachers don't, mostly. He had it in his retirement account. 34 years of a little bit out of every paycheck So the month before, he called the plan and took out the money $26,000 all at once And that money had never been taxed So the next April, all $26,000 counted as income On top of his pension, on top of Social Security Here's what that does And I learned this from Coach himself Two years later, when he came back to my office and sat down with his tax papers to ask me what happened.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b009_.text: First, the income tax on the withdrawal. He was in a higher bracket that year because of it. Second, and nobody knows this one, when your income goes over certain lines, more of your social security becomes taxable. For a married couple, once a certain kind of income passes $32,000, half of your social security can be taxed and pass $44,000 up to 85%. Those numbers have been the same since the 1980s. They never go up. And third, Medicare. If your income one year goes over a certain line, a little over $200,000 for a couple, two years later your Medicare premium goes up. They call it IRMA. It's a surcharge. Most people never hit it, but a big withdrawal in the same year as a house sale or something, it can happen.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b010_.text: Between the extra tax and the extra social security tax, Coach paid around $3,000 to the government that he would not have paid if he had taken a small loan and paid it from his pension a little each month. $3,000 for being a cash buyer. So the rule for us, for retirees, before you take money out of a retirement account to buy a car, you sit down with whoever does your taxes. 30 minutes. Ask one question. If I take this money out this year, what does it cost me? You'd be surprised how many people never ask. Coach never asked. Nobody at the dealership asked him either. Of course not. Okay. Let me stop here because I promised you something. Mrs. Shapiro, this is the second piece. April 1988, Coral Way Motors.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b011_.text: I just closed the door of the finance office because our finance man Sal was out with his gallbladder and Abe told me to do the papers. Mrs. Dottie Shapiro was sitting in the chair across from me in her pink cardigan, her purse on her lap with both hands on it. And she opened the purse and she took out a check, a life insurance check from Irving. And she said, Irving always said, Dottie, never borrow for a car. I want to pay with this. And I looked at that check and I heard Abe's voice in my head. A cash deal in the box is a dead deal. No reserve. Nothing to put in the payment. And I was 24, no, I was 34 years old. And I wanted to impress Abe. So I leaned forward and I said the kindest, most dangerous sentence I ever said in my life. Mrs. Shapiro, keep Irving's money in the bank. That's your cushion. Irving would want you to have a cushion.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b012_.text: Let me get you a nice small payment instead. And she cried a little. And she said, you're so kind, Hector. And she put the check back in her purse. And I slid the papers across the desk. Now hear me. Everything I'm telling you today is that you should probably not walk in and pay cash. And that's exactly what I told Mrs. Shapiro. So what's the difference? Why was I wrong with her and right with you? Hold that thought. The answer is reason number 10. And it's everything. Reason number four, cash is oxygen when you're retired. Marisol, my wife, has one rule in our house that's older than our marriage. The hurricane money doesn't get touched, never. Not for a car, not for a cruise, not for the grandkids. And in September 2017, Hurricane Irma came through and a piece of our neighbor's oak tree came through our roof in Westchester. The roof was $14,000.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b013_.text: The insurance deductible alone in Florida, a hurricane deductible is a percentage of the house. It was more than $5,000. And we paid it the next week from the hurricane money. No loan, no begging, no waiting. When you're working, if you spend your savings, you can earn it back. When you're retired, the money you have is mostly the money you're going to have. You spend $26,000 on a car, and next year your roof goes, or your teeth go, or your husband needs a home aid for three months. and now you're borrowing anyway. Only now it's a credit card at 24% instead of a car loan at 5%. So before any car, ask yourself, after I pay for this, how many months of life do I still have in the bank? If the answer makes your stomach hurt, a small loan is not a weakness, it's a seatbelt. Reason number five, your money can work while the loan is cheap.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b014_.text: This one's simple math. Not always true, but true more often than people think. Let's say a credit union gives you a car loan at 5.9%, and your money sits in a savings account or a certificate at the bank. Some years the bank pays you 1%, then the loan doesn't make sense. Pay down more. But in years when the bank pays 4, 4.5%, the difference is small. and sometimes the car company offers 0% or 1.9 and now it's not even close. You borrow at zero, your money earns four in the bank. On $25,000, 4% is about $1,000 a year for doing nothing. Abe used to say, Hector, banks are smart. They never use their own money. He meant the dealership, but it works for you too. Reason number six, the envelope of hundreds. This one is from the old days, but people still do it.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b015_.text: 1979, Coral Way Motors. A man came in with a cigar box, literally a cigar box, the wooden kind from a factory in Ybo City. And inside, $11,000 in 20s and 50s. He put it on Abe's desk. And Abe counted it twice and smiled and charged him full sticker. Because Abe knew, a man who carries a cigar box of cash across Miami doesn't want questions. He doesn't negotiate. He wants to be gone. Today, here's something you should know. When a dealer receives more than $10,000 in physical cash, real bills, in one deal, the dealer has to report it to the IRS on a form, Form 8300. It's not a crime to pay cash. It's not a problem if your money is clean But it's paperwork And it's a reason, honestly To never carry a bag of money onto a car lot And please, never split it into smaller piles To stay under the $10,000

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b016_.text: That part is a crime. People don't know. They think they're being clever. Pay with a cashier's check or a transfer from your bank. And only when the price is signed. Okay, here's where I'll tell you the rest of what Coach Willis lost. Because we're at about $4,500 now. $1,000 on the price, $2,500 rebate. $3,000 in taxes, give or take. But there was one more piece. And it happened in my office. Reason number seven. The cash buyer gets hit harder in the box. When you finance, I make money from the bank. When you pay cash, I don't. And I still had a quota. Every finance manager in America has a number he has to hit every month. A number per car. So when a cash buyer sat in my chair, I knew this was my only shot. No reserve, no payment. Only the products.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b017_.text: The service contract, the paint and fabric protection, the tire and wheel, the anti-theft etching on the windows, and I pushed harder on a cash buyer than on anybody because that was the only way I was getting paid on that car. Coach Willis bought a 7-year service contract that afternoon, $1,495, plus the paint protection, $595. He wrote me a second check for the products, on a car that had a factory warranty for three years and probably needed nothing else for six. And Coach said, well Hector, at least it's paid for. At least I don't owe anybody. And I said, that's right Coach. And he went home, a little over $6,000 lighter than he had to be. Let me add it for you. $1,000 on the price, $2,500 in rebate, about $3,000 in taxes, and $2,000 in products he didn't need.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b018_.text: $8,000 and change if you count the products. $6,000 if you don't. Either way. So if you're paying cash or financing, it doesn't matter. The answer in the box is the same. You bring the buyer's order I told you about in the last video. The paper with the out-the-door price. And anything that's not on that paper, the answer is no, thank you. And if you want a service contract, you can buy one later. Most of them can be bought anytime before the factory warranty ends. You don't have to decide in that little room. I'll tell you how to read one in this series. There's a lot in the fine print. Reason number eight, you lose the one weapon you have at the end. Here's something I learned on the other side. When you finance, there is a moment after you sign when the dealer needs the bank to say yes. The deal isn't really done for the dealer until the bank buys the contract.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b019_.text: And if you're a careful customer with your own pre-approval in your pocket and they try to change something, you can say, fine, I'll use my credit union. And they lose the whole fifth box. That's power. That's leverage. When you hand them a check, you hand them everything. The money's in their account Monday. If something isn't right, a scratch they promised to fix, the second key they said they'd mail you, the floor mats, it's in the we owe, the little paper where the dealer writes what he said. still owes you, it's now on their schedule, not yours. There's one more side to this. In some deals, the bank can call back and say, the deal didn't go through, come back and sign at a higher rate. That's a trick, a nasty one, and it's coming in the next video with the other tricks of the box.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b020_.text: But for today, just know, the loan from your own credit union, approved before you walk in, protects you from that too. Reason number nine, watch out for a penalty for paying early. Now, I'm going to tell you in a minute to finance and pay it off early. So I have to tell you the danger first. Most car loans today are simple interest. You pay interest only on what you still owe, day by day. If you pay it off in three months, you pay three months of interest. small, but some contracts, especially at buy here, pay here lots, and some older contracts, have a penalty for paying early. Or they use a method that front loads the interest. So before you sign, you look for two words on the contract, prepayment penalty, and you ask out loud, is this simple interest, and is there any penalty if I pay it off early? You want two answers, yes and no. Write them on the buyer's order. Initial them,

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b021_.text: Before I give you number 10, let me tell you about the only customer who ever did it to me perfectly. Not the Alvarez couple from Hialeah. They're a different story, and you'll hear their three words later in this series. This was Mr. Leonard Katz, retired pharmacist from Pinecrest. March 2013. Quiet man, bow tie, a little leather folder. He came into my office at Bird Road, and before I said a word, he opened the folder. inside three papers, a signed buyer's order with the out-the-door price, a letter from his credit union approved at 3.9, and a printout of the manufacturer's offer, 0.9% for 60 months with a $1,000 finance bonus. And he said, Mr. Valdez, I'd like to take your 0.9 and the bonus. I won't need anything else today. Thank you. I tried. Of course I tried. I was good.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b022_.text: I showed him the menu, I told him about the hurricanes, I told him what a transmission cost. And every time he said the same thing very softly, no thank you, I'm fine. Eleven times I counted afterwards, eleven no thank yous. And he signed and he shook my hand and he left. And I found out later from the lender, because we got a notice, that he paid off the entire loan on the fourth month, exactly the fourth month. I sat there with that notice and I laughed out loud in my office alone. Because that little pharmacist had beaten the whole fifth box with a leather folder. Abe would have hated him. I loved him. And reason number 10, the one nobody does, the answer to Mrs. Shapiro. Here's the play, start to finish. You walk in with your money in the bank and a pre-approval from your credit union in your pocket. You don't say cash. You don't say finance.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b023_.text: You say, I haven't decided, let's agree on the price. You get the out-the-door price sign. Then and only then, you ask, is there any rebate or discount if I finance with you? If yes, you take it, you finance. At their bank, at their rate. If it's good, and if it's not good, at yours. Then you go in the box, and you say no to every product that's not on your paper. No thank you, no thank you. Then you go home, you make your first three payments. on time, every one, from your checking account, and on the fourth month, you call the lender yourself, you ask for the payoff amount, and you pay off the whole loan with the money that was sitting in your bank earning interest the whole time. Why three payments? Because some lenders take back the dealer's reserve if the loan is paid off in the first few months. Three payments keeps everybody honest and keeps your credit report looking clean.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b024_.text: It costs you a little interest, a few hundred dollars, maybe less. And for those few hundred dollars, you got the rebate, you got the discount for the finance deal, and you never touched your hurricane money until you decided to. Coach would have kept more than $4,000 in his pocket. Now, why was I wrong with Mrs. Shapiro when I'm telling you basically the same thing? because of one thing. Who's holding the pen? When I told Mrs. Shapiro to keep Irving's check and take a small payment, I wasn't protecting her cushion. I was opening the fifth box. I needed a payment so I had somewhere to hide things and I hid something in there. What I hid, how much it was, and why she never noticed, I'll tell you in this series. I can't do it all today. My hands are shaking just telling you this much. When you finance the way I just told you, you're holding the pen.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b025_.text: You decide the price, you decide the products, you decide the payoff. The loan is just a tool, a hammer. A hammer can build a house or break a window. It depends on whose hand it's in. And you want to know what I do myself? Because that's fair. You should ask that of anybody who gives you advice. Ask him, what do you do? Mary Sol has never, in 44 years of marriage, let me buy a new car. Never. 40 years selling new cars and I drive a used one. She says, Hector, a new car loses a big piece of its value the minute you drive it off the lot. You told me so yourself in 1978. And she's right. So in 2019, when her old car finally died in the parking lot of the Publix on Bird Road, In August, of course, we bought a three-year-old sedan, one owner, from a dealership up in Broward where nobody knew me. And I did exactly what I just told you.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b026_.text: I didn't say cash. I got the price sign. The dealer had a used car special right through their bank, a little lower than my credit union. So I took it. I said no to everything in the box. The young finance man was very good, very polite. He tried to tie and wheel twice. Marisol was sitting next to me. And every time he started a sentence, she just looked at me, that look. That's all she had to do. And I said, no, thank you, son. Then we made three payments. And the fourth month I paid it off from the savings. And the hurricane money? Didn't touch it. Never touched it. Marisol checked. That's what I do. That's what I'd do if I were you. Let me give you the nine quick plus the tenth so you can write them down. One, the moment you say cash, they stop discounting. So you say, I haven't decided. Let's agree on the price. Two, some rebates and discounts only exist if you finance.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b027_.text: Ask and write the answer down. Three, before you take money from a retirement account, ask your tax person what it cost you this year, Social Security and Medicare included. Four, cash is oxygen when you're retired. Keep your hurricane money. Five, when the loan is cheap and the bank pays well, your money can work while you pay slowly. Six, never carry a bag of cash onto a lot. Cashier's check or transfer only after the price is signed. 7. The cash buyer gets pushed harder in the box. Everything not on your paper is a no. 8. A pre-approval from your credit union is your weapon at the end. A check gives the weapon away. 9. Simple interest, no prepayment penalty. Ask out loud and initial it. And 10. Finance to get the deal, three payments, then pay it off. You hold the pen. You know, Coach Willis came back to see me in 2008 with his tax papers.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b028_.text: He sat in my chair, the same chair, and he spread out the papers and he said, Hector, my accountant says I paid $3,000 because I took that money out. Why didn't anybody tell me? And I didn't have an answer for him. I was the finance manager. That was my job, to know. And I knew. And I said nothing because a cash deal was easier for the salesman. And I was busy that Saturday. Coach shook my hand again. He said, it's not your fault, son. It was a little bit my fault. That's why I'm telling you. Now in the box I had a desk drawer, top right. And in that drawer I had a sheet of paper, the menu, and a pen, a heavy pen, and a little calculator I never let the customer see. And with those three things I had ten tricks. Ten. I used them on seniors more than anybody else. Because seniors are polite and seniors trust a man with gray hair and a nice tie.

D:\\wt\\enhc02\\vlog\\enhc02\\voz\\b029_.text: In the next video, I'm going to open that drawer and show you all 10. The menu, the bank callback, the payment that grows while you blink, everyone. And the 10th one is the one I used on Mrs. Shapiro. You'll see it. Subscribe so you don't miss it. And tell me in the comments, did a dealer ever tell you that you'd get a better deal paying cash? The exact words. I'll tell you if it's true. I read everyone. Marisol says that's my new job. She's right. I'll see you in the box.
